Their colleagues told them that the *average* final exam score across all students, $\mu$, varies Normally from year to year with a mean of 80 points and a standard deviation of 4. Further, individual students’ scores Y vary Normally around $\mu$ with a known standard deviation of 3 points. :::::{.my-theorem} :::{.my-theorem-header} :::::: {#thm-005-derivation-posterior-variance-mean} : Step-by-Step Derivation of Posterior Variance and Mean :::::: ::: ::::{.my-theorem-container} ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **1. Starting Point: Bayes' Theorem for Normal Data** ::: When we observe data $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ from a Normal distribution, Bayes' theorem gives us: $$p(\mu \mid \text{data}) \propto p(\text{data} \mid \mu) \cdot p(\mu)$$ For the Normal-Normal model: - **Prior:** $p(\mu) = \mathcal{N}(\theta, \tau^2)$ - **Likelihood:** $p(y_i \mid \mu) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ for each observation *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 1: Write Out the Proportionality** ::: The posterior is proportional to the product of the prior and likelihood: $$p(\mu \mid \text{data}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(\mu - \theta)^2}{2\tau^2}\right) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^{n} \exp\left(-\frac{(y_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$ Combining the exponentials: $$p(\mu \mid \text{data}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(\mu - \theta)^2}{2\tau^2} - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(y_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 2: Expand the Exponent** ::: Let's expand both squared terms in the exponent: $$-\frac{(\mu - \theta)^2}{2\tau^2} - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(y_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}$$ $$= -\frac{\mu^2 - 2\mu\theta + \theta^2}{2\tau^2} - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{y_i^2 - 2y_i\mu + \mu^2}{2\sigma^2}$$ $$= -\frac{\mu^2}{2\tau^2} + \frac{2\mu\theta}{2\tau^2} - \frac{\theta^2}{2\tau^2} - \frac{n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{2\mu\sum y_i}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sum y_i^2}{2\sigma^2}$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 3: Collect Terms by Powers of $\mu$** ::: Group by $\mu^2$, $\mu^1$, and $\mu^0$ (constants): $$= -\frac{\mu^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\right) + \mu\left(\frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{\sum y_i}{\sigma^2}\right) - \left(\frac{\theta^2}{2\tau^2} + \frac{\sum y_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$$ The last term (constants) doesn't affect the shape of the posterior, so we drop it: $$\propto -\frac{\mu^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\right) + \mu\left(\frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{\sum y_i}{\sigma^2}\right)$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 4: Recognize the Normal Form** ::: This is the exponent of a Normal distribution. Recall that a Normal with mean $\mu_n$ and variance $\tau_n^2$ has the form: $$\propto \exp\left(-\frac{(\mu - \mu_n)^2}{2\tau_n^2}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{\mu^2 - 2\mu\mu_n + \mu_n^2}{2\tau_n^2}\right)$$ $$\propto \exp\left(-\frac{\mu^2}{2\tau_n^2} + \frac{\mu\mu_n}{\tau_n^2}\right)$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 5: Match Coefficients** ::: We have from Step 3: $$\propto -\frac{\mu^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\right) + \mu\left(\frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{\sum y_i}{\sigma^2}\right)$$ And from the standard Normal form: $$\propto -\frac{\mu^2}{2\tau_n^2} + \frac{\mu\mu_n}{\tau_n^2}$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Match Coefficient of $\mu^2$:** ::: $$\frac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}$$ This gives us the **posterior precision** (inverse variance). Solving for posterior variance: $$\boxed{\tau_n^2 = \frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\tau^2} + \dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}}}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Match Coefficient of $\mu$:** ::: $$\frac{\mu_n}{\tau_n^2} = \frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{\sum y_i}{\sigma^2}$$ Now solve for $\mu_n$: $$\mu_n = \tau_n^2 \left( \frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{\sum y_i}{\sigma^2} \right)$$ But since $\sum y_i = n \bar{y}$, we can write: $$\boxed{\mu_n = \tau_n^2 \left( \frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{n \bar{y}}{\sigma^2} \right)}$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 6: Alternative Form — Weighted Average** ::: We can also write the posterior mean as a **precision-weighted average** of prior mean and sample mean: Let’s define: - Prior precision: $P_0 = \frac{1}{\tau^2}$ - Data precision: $P_n = \frac{n}{\sigma^2}$ Then: $$\mu_n = \frac{P_0 \cdot \theta + P_n \cdot \bar{y}}{P_0 + P_n}$$ This shows the posterior mean is a **weighted average** of the prior mean and the sample mean, where weights are the respective precisions. *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Summary of Final Formulas** ::: | Quantity | Formula | |----------|---------| | **Posterior variance** | $\tau_n^2 = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\tau^2} + \dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}}$ | | **Posterior mean** | $\mu_n = \tau_n^2 \left( \dfrac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \dfrac{n \bar{y}}{\sigma^2} \right)$ | | **Alternative mean** | $\mu_n = \dfrac{\dfrac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \dfrac{n \bar{y}}{\sigma^2}}{\dfrac{1}{\tau^2} + \dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}}$ | :::: ::::: :::::{.my-exercise} :::{.my-exercise-header} :::::: {#exr-005-normal-normal-cacluation} : Normal-Normal calculation :::::: ::: ::::{.my-exercise-container} **a) Prof. Abebe** conducts the final exam and observes that his 32 students scored an average of 86 points. Calculate the posterior mean and variance of $\mu$ using the data from Prof. Abebe’s class. Specify the posterior model of $\mu$: - our Normal prior model of $\mu$ had mean $\theta = 80$ and standard deviation $\tau = 4$; - our $n = 32$ students taking the final exam scored at average 86 points; - individual students’ scores $Y$ vary Normally around $\mu$ with a known standard deviation of 3 points. *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 150%"} **Bayesian Updating for Prof. Abebe's Class** ::: ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Setting Up the Model** ::: This is a classic **Normal-Normal conjugate model**. We have: | Component | Distribution | Mean | Std / Variance | |-----------|-------------|------|----------------| | Prior on $\mu$ | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \tau^2)$ | $\theta = 80$ | $\tau = 4$, $\tau^2 = 16$ | | Likelihood (individual scores) | $Y_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma = 3$, $\sigma^2 = 9$ | | Observed data | $n = 32$ students | $\bar{y} = 86$ | — | *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **The Normal-Normal Posterior Formula** ::: When the prior on $\mu$ is Normal and the likelihood is Normal with **known** $\sigma^2$, the posterior is also Normal (conjugacy). The general formulas are: $$\mu \mid \bar{y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_n,\, \tau_n^2\right)$$ **Posterior variance:** $$\tau_n^2 = \frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\tau^2} + \dfrac{n}{\sigma^2}}$$ **Posterior mean:** $$\mu_n = \tau_n^2 \left(\frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{n\bar{y}}{\sigma^2}\right)$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 1 — Compute the Posterior Variance** ::: The posterior precision is the **sum of the prior precision and the data precision**: $$ \begin{align*} \frac{1}{\tau_n^2} &= \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2} \\ &= \frac{1}{16} + \frac{32}{9} \\ &= 0.0625 + 3.5\overline{5} = 3.618\overline{05} \\ \tau_n^2 &= \frac{1}{3.618\overline{05}} \\ &=\boxed{ 0.276392} \end{align*} $$ {#eq-005-exr-exams-posterior-variance} > **Intuition:** The posterior variance is *much* smaller than the prior variance ($\tau^2 = 16$), because 32 observations carry a lot of information, sharply concentrating our beliefs about $\mu$. *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 2 — Compute the Posterior Mean** ::: The posterior mean is a **precision-weighted average** of the prior mean and the sample mean: $$ \begin{align*} &\mu_n = \tau_n^2 \left(\frac{\theta}{\tau^2} + \frac{n\bar{y}}{\sigma^2}\right) \\ &= 0.2764\left(\frac{80}{16} + \frac{32 \times 86}{9}\right) \\ &= 0.276422 \left(5 + 305.777778\right) \\ &= 0.276422 \times 310.777778 \\ &\boxed{\approx 85.8964} \end{align*} $$ {#eq-005-exr-exams-posterior-mean} *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Step 3 — Intuition: Shrinkage Toward the Prior** ::: The posterior mean can be rewritten as a **weighted blend** of the prior mean and the data: $$\mu_n = (1-w)\,\theta + w\,\bar{y}$$ where the weight on the data is: $$w = \frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2 + n/\sigma^2} = \frac{3.5\overline{5}}{3.618\overline{05}} \approx 0.9827$$ So: $$ \begin{align*} \mu_n &= ((1 - 0.9827255) \cdot 80) + (0.9827255 \cdot 86) \\ &= 1.38196 + 84.51439 \\ &=\boxed{ 85.89635} \end{align*} $$ {#eq-005-exr-shrinkage-toward-prior} $$\mu_n = (1 - 0.9827)(80) + (0.9827)(86) = 0.1396 + 85.70 \approx 85.84 ✓$$ > **Intuition:** With 32 students and a tight likelihood ($\sigma=3$), the data dominate (~98.3% weight). The posterior mean of **85.84** is pulled only slightly from the observed $\bar{y} = 86$ back toward the prior mean of 80 — this *shrinkage* is a hallmark of Bayesian inference. *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Summary** ::: | Quantity | Value | |----------|-------| | Prior mean $\theta$ | 80 | | Observed sample mean $\bar{y}$ | 86 | | **Posterior mean** $\mu_n$ | **85.89644** | | **Posterior variance** $\tau_n^2$ | **0.276392** | | Posterior std $\tau_n$ | ≈ 0.526 | ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Bayesian updating with `bayesrules::summarize_normal_normal()`** ::: :::::{.my-r-code} :::{.my-r-code-header} :::::: {#cnj-005-exr-bayesian-updating-abebe} : Bayesian updating for Prof. Abebe’s class :::::: ::: ::::{.my-r-code-container} ::: {#tbl-005-exr-prof-abebe .cell tbl-cap='Bayesian updating for Prof. Abebe’s class'} ```{.r .cell-code} bayesrules::summarize_normal_normal( mean = 80, sd = 4, sigma = 3, y_bar = 86, n = 32) |> knitr::kable(digits = 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |model | mean| mode| var| sd| |:---------|-------:|-------:|-------:|------:| |prior | 80.0000| 80.0000| 16.0000| 4.0000| |posterior | 85.8964| 85.8964| 0.2764| 0.5257| ::: ::: :::: ::::: **Calculating manually and via bayesrules::summarize_normal_normal() gives the same results.** *** **b) Prof. Morales** conducts the final exam and observes that her 32 students scored an average of 82 points. The range of 10 to 50°C is **symmetric around 30°C**, spanning **±20°C** from the mean: $$\theta = 30, \quad \text{range} = [10, 50]$$ The most natural interpretation of *"anywhere between 10 and 50"* is that this represents **virtually all** of the prior probability mass, i.e., **~4 standard deviations on each side (99.99% rule):** $$ \begin{align*} \theta \pm 4\sigma &= [10, 50] \\ 4\sigma &= 20 \implies \boxed{\sigma = 5} \end{align*} $$ Depending on how strictly you read *"anywhere between"*, you could also use: | Rule | Interpretation | Equation | $\sigma$ | |------|---------------|----------|----------| | $\pm 2\sigma$ | 95% of values | $2\sigma = 20$ | 10 | | $\pm 3\sigma$ | 99.7% of values | $3\sigma = 20$ | 6.67 | | **$\pm 4\sigma$** | **~99.99% of values** | **$4\sigma = 20$** | **5** | The **$\pm 4\sigma$ rule ($\sigma = 5$)** is the standard choice here because it treats the stated range as containing **nearly all** plausible values, which best matches the phrase *"might be anywhere between"*. So our prior model is $$\boxed{Y_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N} (30, 5^2)}$$. :::::{.my-r-code} :::{.my-r-code-header} :::::: {#cnj-005-exr-prior-model-australia} : Normal prior for $\mu$ reflecting our friend’s understanding of Australian weather :::::: ::: ::::{.my-r-code-container} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayesrules::plot_normal(mean = 30, sd = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Normal prior for μ reflecting our friend’s understanding of Australian weather](005-conjugate-families_files/figure-html/fig-005-exr-prior-model-australia-1.png){#fig-005-exr-prior-model-australia width=672} ::: ::: :::: ::::: **b) The `weather_perth` data in the {bayesrules} package includes 1000 daily observations of 3 p.m. temperatures in Perth (`temp3pm`). I had great problems to understand which value I should take for the standard deviation of the posterior model? At first I thought I should take `sd(weather_perth$temp3pm)` = 5.8297818. I saw a discrepancy arising because we're working with **two different sources of variability**: | Component | Standard Deviation | What It Measures | |-----------|-------------------|-----------------| | **Prior assumption** $\sigma$ | 5°C | Daily variation *around* the true mean $\mu$ | | **Sample sd** | 5.8298°C | Observed variation in the 1000 daily temperatures | After a conversation with Claude Haiku I understood that I have to take the **standard deviation of the model: sd = 5** The **sample standard deviation of 5.8298°C** is an *estimate* of the **population standard deviation** $\sigma$ (the daily variation around the true mean). It differs from our assumed $\sigma = 5$ for several reasons: 1. **Sampling variability:** The sample sd is computed from 1000 observations and will naturally fluctuate around the true population value. 2. **Our assumption may be slightly off:** We assumed $\sigma = 5$ based on the model specification, but the actual daily variation in Perth temperatures might be slightly higher (5.83°C). 3. **The sample sd is not used in the posterior calculation:** In the Bayesian model with **known** $\sigma$, we treat $\sigma = 5$ as **fixed and given**, not estimated from the data. The posterior depends only on: - The prior ($\theta = 30$, $\tau = 5$) - The sample mean ($\bar{y} = 24.0009$) - The assumed likelihood sd ($\sigma = 5$, treated as known) **The sample sd of 5.8298 is informative but serves a different purpose:** - **If we were uncertain about $\sigma$:** We could use the sample sd to estimate it or construct a credible interval for $\sigma$. - **For model checking:** A sample sd of 5.83 vs. our assumed 5 suggests the model assumption is reasonable but slightly conservative (the data show slightly more daily variation than assumed). - **For sensitivity analysis:** We could re-run the posterior with $\sigma = 5.83$ to see how robust our conclusions are. 1. The posterior calculation has to be $\sigma = 5$ because it is a **model assumption** (the likelihood standard deviation), not something we estimate from the data. 2. The sample sd of 5.8298 is a **descriptive statistic** that validates our assumption is in the right ballpark, but it doesn't change the posterior under the Normal-Normal conjugate model with known $\sigma$. So the answer which sd to use lies in the provided **model specification**: > “… they’ll assume that daily temperatures vary Normally around $\mu$ with a standard deviation of 5 degrees: $Y_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, 5^2)$.” This means: ✅ **$\sigma = 5$ is a fixed, known parameter** in the model — **not estimated from the data**. In Bayesian inference, when we say “known $\sigma$”, we are assuming: - The variability of daily temperatures around the true mean $\mu$ is **exactly 5°C**. - We are **not using the sample standard deviation (5.8298)** to estimate $\sigma$. - The posterior for $\mu$ is computed **conditional on this fixed $\sigma = 5$**. This is called the **Normal-Normal conjugate model with known variance** — a standard textbook setup. The sample standard deviation of 5.8298 is: - An **empirical estimate** of the population $\sigma$ based on 1000 observations. - A **descriptive statistic** — it tells us what the data *actually* show. - **Not used in the posterior calculation** under the assumption that $\sigma$ is known. We could use sd = 5.8298 instead --- but that would be a **different model**: - We would need to treat $\sigma$ as **unknown** and estimate it (e.g., using a Normal-Gamma model). - Or, we could do a **sensitivity analysis** and recompute the posterior with $\sigma = 5.8298$ to see how much it changes. But **under the model that was specified**, $\sigma = 5$ is fixed — so we use it. ::: Taking the result of @nte-005-exr-perth-weather-posterior-model we get for the posterior model of $\mu$: - our Normal prior model of $\mu$ had mean $\theta = 30$ and standard deviation $\tau = 5$; Prior: $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(30, 25)$ — centered at 30°C with wide uncertainty Posterior: $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(24.01, 0.0250)$ — centered at 24°C with very tight uncertainty The data revealed that Perth's average 3 p.m. temperature is ~6°C cooler than our friend initially believed. Extreme Precision The posterior standard deviation is only 0.158°C this is an extreme precision, meaning we're now 95% confident that $\mu$ lies in: $$24.01 \pm 1.96(0.158) = 24.01 \pm 0.31 = [23.70, 24.32] \text{ degrees}$$ With 1000 observations, the sample mean (24.0009) nearly equals the posterior mean (24.01), with only minimal shrinkage toward the prior mean of 30. The weight on the data is ~99.9%, while the prior receives ~0.1% weight! :::::{.my-theorem} :::{.my-theorem-header} :::::: {#thm-005-exr-calculate-weight-and-data-prior} : Calculating the weight of the data in comparison with the prior pdf :::::: ::: ::::{.my-theorem-container} ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **The Weighted Average Formula** ::: Recall from the derivation that the posterior mean can be written as a **precision-weighted average**: $$ \begin{align*} \mu_n = (1-w)\,\theta + w\,\bar{y} \\ \text{where w is the weight on the data} \\ w = \frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/\tau^2 + n/\sigma^2} \end{align*} $$ {#eq-005-exr-precision-weighted-average} ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Plugging In the Numbers** ::: **Numerator** (data precision): $$\frac{n}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1000}{25} = 40$$ **Denominator** (total precision = prior precision + data precision): $$\frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{n}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{25} + \frac{1000}{25} = \frac{1001}{25} = 40.04$$ **Weight on the data:** $$w = \frac{40}{40.04} \approx 0.99900 \approx 99.9\%$$ **Weight on the prior:** $$1 - w = \frac{0.04}{40.04} \approx 0.00100 \approx 0.1\%$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **The weight of the data in comparison with the prior pdf for the weather in Perth** ::: | Component | Weight | |-----------|--------| | **Data** $\bar{y}$ | **~99.9%** | | **Prior** $\theta$ | **~0.1%** | **Verification** $$ \begin{align*} \mu_n &= (1-w)\,\theta + w\,\bar{y} \\ &= 0.001(30) + 0.999(24.0009) \\ &= 0.030 + 23.977 \\ &= 24.007 ✓ \end{align*} $$ {#eq-005-exr-verification-precision-weighted-average} This confirms that with 1000 observations and equal $\tau = \sigma = 5$, the data almost completely dominate the posterior. :::: ::::: :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-note #nte-005-exr-bayesian-advantages} ###### When Bayesian Inference Shines Given the dominate role data plays the question arose for me: What is the advantage of using the Bayesian approach? Frequentist statistics would get almost the same result. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 140%"} **Advantages of the Bayesian approach** ::: ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 120%"} **1. Small Sample Sizes** ::: With only **10 or 50 days** of data instead of 1000, the prior would carry meaningful weight: **Example: $n = 50$ days** $$w = \frac{50/25}{1/25 + 50/25} = \frac{2}{2.04} \approx 0.98 \text{ (98% data)}$$ Weight on prior: **~2%** — now the prior actually matters! The Bayesian posterior would be: $$\mu_n \approx 0.02(30) + 0.98(\bar{y})$$ This **regularizes** the estimate when data are scarce, preventing wild swings from small samples. Frequentist confidence intervals would be much wider and less informative. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 120%"} **2. Incorporating Prior Knowledge** ::: Our friend's prior belief (30°C, sd = 5) encodes real information: - Perth is in the Southern Hemisphere (warmer than many places) - 3 p.m. is afternoon (warmer than morning) - The range [10, 50] reflects reasonable bounds **Frequentist approach:** Ignores this entirely. If the first 50 observations happened to average 18°C due to sampling variability, the frequentist estimate would be 18°C with no skepticism. **Bayesian approach:** Would say "18°C is implausibly cold given what we know about Perth" and pull the estimate back toward 30°C. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 120%"} **3. Decision-Making Under Uncertainty** ::: Suppose your friend needs to decide: *"Should I bring a light jacket (assume μ ≥ 22°C) or a heavy coat (assume μ < 22°C)?"* **Bayesian:** Directly answers: $P(\mu \geq 22 \mid \text{data}) = ?$ With posterior $\mu \mid \text{data} \sim \mathcal{N}(24.01, 0.158^2)$: $$P(\mu \geq 22 \mid \text{data}) = P\left(Z \geq \frac{22 - 24.01}{0.158}\right) = P(Z \geq -12.7) \approx 1.0$$ **Frequentist:** Cannot directly answer this. A 95% CI is [23.70, 24.32], but that doesn't directly tell you $P(\mu \geq 22)$ in a frequentist framework. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 120%"} **4. Hierarchical/Complex Models** ::: With multiple professors, multiple cities, or temporal trends, Bayesian methods naturally handle: - Sharing information across groups - Partial pooling of estimates - Uncertainty propagation through layers Frequentist approaches become awkward or require ad-hoc methods. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 120%"} **5. Sequential Analysis** ::: Suppose you observe data on Day 1, then Day 2, then Day 3... **Bayesian:** Today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior. You naturally update beliefs as new data arrive — no multiple testing corrections needed. **Frequentist:** Each new test inflates Type I error; you need corrections (Bonferroni, etc.), making inference less efficient. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 140%"} **Why This Exercise Didn't Show Bayesian Advantage** ::: In the Perth temperature problem: - ✅ Large sample size ($n = 1000$) → data overwhelm the prior - ✅ Prior and likelihood have equal information ($\tau = \sigma$) - ✅ Simple one-parameter model - ✅ No sequential or hierarchical structure In this setting, Bayesian and frequentist methods converge — and that's **expected and fine**. **Bayesian inference adds the most value when:** - Data are limited - Prior knowledge is informative and relevant - You need probability statements about parameters (not just intervals) - You're making sequential decisions - You have complex hierarchical structures **When data are abundant and prior is weak, Bayesian and frequentist results converge** — which is reassuring, not a weakness! ::: #### Normal-Normal Simulation :::::{.my-exercise} :::{.my-exercise-header} :::::: {#exr-005-exr-normal-normal-simulation} : Normal-Normal Simulation :::::: ::: ::::{.my-exercise-container} **a) Your friend Alex has read @sec-chap-004 of this book, but not this chapter. Explain to Alex why it’s difficult to simulate a Normal-Normal posterior using the simulation methods we have learned thus far.** Simulating the Normal-Normal example with the methods learned so far is not possible. We have seen in @prp-005-steps-of-simulations that we must follow four steps to simulate the Normal-Normal model. The problem arises with step 3: > Filter out only those of the $10000$ simulated sets of $(θ, Y )$ for which the simulated $Y$ data matches the data we actually observed. This doesn't work with the Normal-Normal model: We won't have any match, because our data values $Y_i$ are continuous! **b) To prove your point, try (and fail) to simulate the posterior of μ for the following model upon observing a single data point $Y = 1.1$: $$ \begin{align*} Y \mid \mu &\sim \mathcal{N} (\mu, 1^2) \\ \mu &\sim \mathcal{N} (0.1^2) \end{align*} $$ {#eq-005-exr-normal-normal-example} ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Why This Simulation Method Fails for Normal-Normal Models** ::: The fundamental problem is **the curse of continuous data**: when you simulate data from a continuous distribution, the probability of generating data that *exactly matches* your observed value is essentially **zero**. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **The Core Issue** ::: In step 3, you're filtering for simulated $Y$ values that match your observed $Y = 1.1$ *exactly*. But since $Y$ is continuous: $$P(Y_{\text{simulated}} = 1.1 \text{ exactly}) \approx 0$$ This means virtually **none** of your 10,000 simulated ($\theta$, $Y$) pairs will pass the filter, leaving you with an empty (or nearly empty) posterior sample. *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Demonstration: Attempting to Simulate the Posterior** ::: Let me show why this fails with the following model: **Prior:** $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1^2)$ **Likelihood:** $Y \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1^2)$ **Observed:** $Y = 1.1$ :::::{.my-assessment} :::{.my-assessment-header} :::::: {#cor-005-exr-simulate-posterior} : Simulate the Posterior pdf :::::: ::: ::::{.my-assessment-container} - **Step 1**: Simulate 10,000 theta values from prior - **Step 2**: Simulate data Y from each theta - **Step 3**: Filter for exact match to observed Y = 1.1 - **Step 4**: Extract posterior theta values :::: ::::: **R Code (tidyverse style)** ::: {#tbl-005-failed-simulation-1 .cell tbl-cap='Failed simulation with 0 matches'} ```{.r .cell-code} base::set.seed(84735) Y_observed <- 1.1 n_sims <- 10000 posterior_attempt <- tibble::tibble( sim_id = 1:n_sims, # Step 1: Simulate 10,000 theta values from prior ########### theta = stats::rnorm(n_sims, mean = 0, sd = 0.1) ) |> dplyr::mutate( # Step 2: Simulate data Y from each theta ################### Y_simulated = stats::rnorm(n_sims, mean = theta, sd = 1.0) ) |> # Step 3: Filter for exact match to observed Y = 1.1 ######## dplyr::filter(Y_simulated == Y_observed) |> dplyr::select(theta) # Step 4: Extract posterior theta values ############ base::cat("Number of matches:", nrow(posterior_attempt), "\n") base::cat("Posterior sample size:", nrow(posterior_attempt), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Number of matches: 0 #> Posterior sample size: 0 ``` ::: ::: **You get nothing.** Even with 10,000 simulations, you'll have zero (or perhaps one or two by extreme luck) matches. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Why This Happens Mathematically** ::: The probability of a match in any single simulation is: $$P(\text{match}) = \int P(Y_{\text{sim}} = 1.1 \mid Y_{\text{sim}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, 1)) \, dP(\theta)$$ For continuous distributions, this integral is **zero** because the probability density at a single point is infinitesimal. Even with a small tolerance (e.g., $|Y_{\text{sim}} - 1.1| < 0.01$), you'd need an astronomically large number of simulations to get a reasonable posterior sample. ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Attempting a Fix: Adding a Tolerance Window** ::: To illustrate the problem more clearly, here's what happens if you add a small tolerance: :::::{.my-r-code} :::{.my-r-code-header} :::::: {#cnj-005-exr-unreliable-simulation} : Unreliable simulation with only few matches :::::: ::: ::::{.my-r-code-container} ::: {#tbl-005-failed-simulation-2 .cell tbl-cap='Unreliable simulation with just a few matches'} ```{.r .cell-code} base::set.seed(100) Y_observed <- 1.1 n_sims <- 10000 tolerance <- 0.01 # Accept values within ±0.01 posterior_with_tolerance <- tibble::tibble( sim_id = 1:n_sims, # Step 1: Simulate 10,000 theta values from prior ########## theta = stats::rnorm(n_sims, mean = 0, sd = 0.1) ) |> dplyr::mutate( # Step 2: Simulate data Y from each theta ################### Y_simulated = stats::rnorm(n_sims, mean = theta, sd = 1.0) ) |> # Step 3: Filter for exact match to observed Y = 1.1# tolerance ######## dplyr::filter(abs(Y_simulated - Y_observed) < tolerance) |> dplyr::select(theta) # Step 4a: Number of posterior theta values ############ base::cat("Number of matches with tolerance:", nrow(posterior_with_tolerance), "\n") # Step 4a: Extract posterior theta values ############ if (base::nrow(posterior_with_tolerance) > 0) { posterior_with_tolerance |> dplyr::summarize( mean_theta = mean(theta), sd_theta = sd(theta), .groups = "drop" ) |> print() } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Number of matches with tolerance: 32 #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #> mean_theta sd_theta #> #> 1 0.0223 0.111 ``` ::: ::: :::: ::::: Even with a tolerance of 0.01, you'll likely get only few matches (30-50 matches), making the posterior estimate unreliable. **There are three different solutions: For details see: @sec-910-solution-continuous-distribution}** :::: ::::: ### General Practice Exercises #### Which model? :::::{.my-assessment} :::{.my-assessment-header} :::::: {#cor-005-exr-which-model} : Which model? :::::: ::: ::::{.my-assessment-container} Below are kernels for Normal, Poisson, Gamma, Beta, and Binomial models. In @sec-005-normal-normal-conjugacy, we expressed the Normal-Normal posterior mean of $\mu$ as a weighted average of the prior mean $\theta$ and the observed sample mean $y$. Similarly, express the Gamma-Poisson posterior mean of rate $\lambda, E(\lambda \mid \overrightarrow{\rm y})$, as a weighted average of the prior mean $E(\lambda)$ and sample mean $y$. :::::{.my-exercise} :::{.my-exercise-header} :::::: {#exr-005-gamma-poisson-average} : Gamma-Poisson posterior mean as weighted average :::::: ::: ::::{.my-exercise-container} ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Setup** ::: - **Prior:** $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)$ - **Likelihood:** $Y_i \mid \lambda \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ - **Posterior:** $\lambda \mid \vec{y} \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha + \sum y_i, \beta + n)$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Posterior mean** ::: The posterior mean is: $$E(\lambda \mid \vec{y}) = \frac{\alpha + \sum_{i=1}^n y_i}{\beta + n}$$ Rearranging: $$E(\lambda \mid \vec{y}) = \frac{\alpha}{\beta + n} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}{\beta + n}$$ $$E(\lambda \mid \vec{y}) = \frac{\beta}{\beta + n} \cdot \frac{\alpha}{\beta} + \frac{n}{\beta + n} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i}{n}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Weighted Average Form** ::: $$\boxed{E(\lambda \mid \vec{y}) = \frac{\beta}{\beta + n} \cdot E(\lambda) + \frac{n}{\beta + n} \cdot \bar{y}}$$ where: - **$E(\lambda) = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}$** = prior mean - **$\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$** = sample mean - **$\frac{\beta}{\beta + n}$** = prior weight - **$\frac{n}{\beta + n}$** = data weight ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Interpretation** ::: The posterior mean is a **convex combination** of: 1. **Prior mean** ($E(\lambda)$), weighted by $\frac{\beta}{\beta + n}$ 2. **Sample mean** ($\bar{y}$), weighted by $\frac{n}{\beta + n}$ **Key insights:** - As $n \to \infty$: posterior mean → sample mean (data dominates) - As $\beta \to \infty$: posterior mean → prior mean (strong prior belief) - As $\beta \to 0$: posterior mean → sample mean (weak prior) :::: ::::: #### Counting insects A biologist hires you to study the density of a certain insect in the local region. **Prior distribution:** $\theta \sim \text{Gamma}(s, r)$ - **Expected value:** $E[\theta] = 0.5$ - **Standard deviation:** $\text{SD}[\theta] = 0.25$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Gamma Distribution Properties** ::: See @eq-005-gamma-central-measures in @sec-005-gamma-formulas: For $\theta \sim \text{Gamma}(r, s)$: $$ \begin{align*} E[\theta] &= \frac{s}{r} \\ \text{Var}[\theta] &= \frac{s}{r^2} \\ \text{SD}[\theta] &= \sqrt{\frac{s}{r^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{s}}{r} \end{align*} $$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Solving for $s$ and $r$** ::: ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **From the variance relationship:** ::: $$\text{Var}[\theta] = (\text{SD}[\theta])^2 = (0.25)^2 = 0.0625$$ Using $\text{Var}[\theta] = \dfrac{s}{r^2}$: $$\frac{s}{r^2} = 0.0625 \quad \Rightarrow \quad s = 0.0625 r^2 \quad \cdots (1)$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **From the mean relationship:** ::: $$\frac{s}{r} = 0.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad s = 0.5r \quad \cdots (2)$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Equate (1) and (2):** ::: $$0.0625 r^2 = 0.5r$$ $$0.0625 r = 0.5$$ $$r = \frac{0.5}{0.0625} = 8$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Solve for $r$:** ::: $$s = 0.5 \cdot r = 0.5 \cdot 8 = 4$$ *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Answer** ::: $$\boxed{s = 4, \quad r = 8}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **Verification** ::: - If possible, identify the name of the posterior model and its parameters.** ::: ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Bayes’ Theorem Setup** ::: The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior: $$p(\theta \mid y) \propto f(y \mid \theta) \cdot p(\theta)$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Likelihood** ::: Given $Y = y$ with the Geometric distribution: $$f(y \mid \theta) = \theta(1-\theta)^{y-1}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Prior** ::: The Beta prior: $$p(\theta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha + \beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)} \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Deriving the Posterior** ::: Applying Bayes' theorem (keeping only terms involving $\theta$): $$p(\theta \mid y) \propto \theta(1-\theta)^{y-1} \cdot \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}$$ Combining the powers of $\theta$ and ($1-\theta$): $$p(\theta \mid y) \propto \theta^{1+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{y-1+\beta-1}$$ $$p(\theta \mid y) \propto \theta^{\alpha}(1-\theta)^{y+\beta-2}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Posterior Model** ::: This is the kernel of a **Beta distribution**. Specifically: $$\boxed{\theta \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + 1, \beta + y - 1)}$$ ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 110%"} **Summary** ::: | Component | Distribution | Parameters | |-----------|--------------|-----------| | Prior | Beta | $\alpha, \beta$ | | Likelihood | Geometric | θ | | Posterior | Beta | $\alpha + 1, \beta + y - 1$ | *** ::: {#big-text style="font-size: 125%"} **b) Is the Beta model a conjugate prior for the Geometric data model?** ::: **Key insight:** The Beta distribution is the **conjugate prior** for the Geometric likelihood, meaning the posterior remains in the same Beta family. The posterior parameters show that observing a single geometric trial with outcome y increases the first parameter by $1$ and the second parameter by $y - 1$. :::: ::::: ## Glossary Entries {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
Beta-Binomial-Model The Beta-Binomial Bayesian Model is a fundamental framework in Bayesian statistics used to estimate a proportion π (e.g., success probability) when data are binary outcomes (success/failure) across n independent trials. The Beta-Binomial Bayesian Model combines a Beta prior with a Binomial likelihood, resulting in a Beta posterior due to conjugacy. This makes it ideal for estimating unknown proportions (e.g., success rates) from binary data.
Beta-Model The beta model is a statistical model where the response variable follows a Beta distribution, which is appropriate for continuous data bounded between 0 and 1 — such as proportions, percentages, rates, or probabilities. (Brave-AI)
Claude Haiku Claude Haiku is Anthropic’s smallest, fastest, and most cost-effective model in the Claude family, designed for high-speed, low-latency tasks while maintaining strong performance on coding, computer use, and agent workflows.
Conjugate Prior If the [posterior distribution] is in the same probability distribution family as the prior probability distribution the prior and posterior are then called conjugate distributions, and the prior is called a conjugate prior for the likelihood function. A conjugate prior is an algebraic convenience; otherwise, numerical integration may be necessary. (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior">Wikipedia</a>)
Exponential-Model An exponential model describes a process where a quantity changes at a rate proportional to its current value, leading to rapid growth or decay over time. (Bave-AI)
F-Distribution-Model The F model (or F-distribution model) is a statistical model used for testing equality of variances and comparing means across multiple groups. The F-distribution arises from the ratio of two chi-squared distributions. (Brave-AI)
Gamma-Model The Gamma model is a statistical model where the response variable follows a Gamma distribution, which is appropriate for positive continuous data — such as time-to-event, income, insurance claims, or size measurements. (Brave-AI)
Gamma-Poisson Model A Gamma-Poisson model is a hierarchical statistical model that combines two probability distributions to handle overdispersed count data. (a) **The Poisson distribution:** Models the observed counts, with a rate parameter λ (lambda). (b) **The Gamma distribution**: Models the variability in λ itself, treating it as a random variable rather than a fixed parameter. (Brave-AI)
Hyperparameter In the Bayesian framework, a hyperparameter is a parameter of a prior distribution. It defines the shape, location, or scale of the prior belief about a model parameter before observing any data. Unlike model parameters, which are estimated from the data (e.g., the mean or variance of a distribution), hyperparameters are set before the analysis begins and are not directly learned from the data. (Brave-AI)
Joint_Probability_Density_Function Joint Probability Density Function (Joint PDF) is a function used to describe the probability distribution of two or more continuous random variables together. It is denoted as f(x, y) for two random variables X and Y, and provides the probability density at any point (x, y) in the two-dimensional space.
Joint_Probability_Mass_Function The joint probability mass function is a function that completely characterizes the distribution of a discrete random vector. When evaluated at a given point, it gives the probability that the realization of the random vector will be equal to that point. The term 'joint probability function' is often used as a synonym. Sometimes, the abbreviation 'joint pmf' is used. (statlect.com)
Likelihood_x The likelihood refers to the probability of observing the given data under a specific hypothesis or set of parameter values. It is denotated as P(E | H), where E represents the evidence (data) and H represents the hypothesis. The likelihood quantifies how well a statistical model explains the observed data for different parameter values and serves as a critical component in updating beliefs in Bayesian inference. (Brave-AI)
Likelihood-Function The likelihood function measures the plausibility of different parameter values given the observed data, rather than the probability of the data itself. It is not a probability distribution over the parameters, as it does not integrate or sum to one, and it is not normalized. Instead, it quantifies how likely the observed data are under different parameter settings. (Brave-AI)
LLMs Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced artificial intelligence systems trained on massive amounts of text data to understand, generate, and manipulate human language. LLMs function as statistical prediction machines, learning patterns in language by predicting the next word in a sequence. This allows them to perform diverse tasks such as answering questions, writing essays, translating languages, summarizing documents, generating code, and even engaging in conversation. (Brave-AI)
Marginal_Probability Marginal probability refers to the probability of a single event occurring independently, without considering the outcomes of other related events. It is (the same concept) as an unconditional probability, denoted as P(A) or P(B), and is derived from a joint probability distribution by summing or integrating over the other variables involved. A marginal distribution gets it’s name because it appears in the margins of a probability distribution table.
MLE Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a method of estimating the parameters of an assumed probability distribution, given some observed data. This is achieved by maximizing a likelihood function so that, under the assumed statistical model, the observed data is most probable. The point in the parameter space that maximizes the likelihood function is called the maximum likelihood estimate. (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Maximum_likelihood_estimation&oldid=1178502960">Wkipedia</a>)
Normal-Model A normal model in statistics refers to the use of the normal distribution—a symmetric, bell-shaped curve—to describe or approximate the distribution of a continuous variable. It is defined by two parameters: the mean (μ), which determines the center, and the standard deviation (σ), which determines the spread.
Normal-Normal Conjugate Family Normal-Normal Conjugate Family refers to a Bayesian modeling setup where the likelihood is based on a normal distribution with unknown mean μ and known variance, and the prior for μ is also a normal distribution. This combination results in a posterior distribution for μ that is also normal, making it a conjugate family.
Parameter_x Unobserved variables are usually called Parameters. (SR2, Chap.2) A parameter is an unknown numerical characteristics of a population that must be estimated. (CDS). They are also numbers that govern statistical models ([stats.stackexchange](https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/255994/207389)). A parameter is also a number that is a defining characteristic of some population or a feature of a population. (SwR, Glossary)
PDF A probability density function (PDF) describes a probability distribution for a random, continuous variable. Use a probability density function to find the chances that the value of a random variable will occur within a range of values that you specify. More specifically, a PDF is a function where its integral for an interval provides the probability of a value occurring in that interval. (<a href="https://statisticsbyjim.com/probability/probability-density-function/">Statistics By Jim</a>)
Poisson-Model The Poisson model is a fundamental statistical model used for count data — that is, data representing the number of times an event occurs within a fixed interval of time or space. (Brave-AI)
Posterior_Model The posterior model represents the updated beliefs about the parameters of a model after incorporating observed data. It is derived by combining the prior distribution, which reflects initial beliefs about the parameter, with the likelihood of the observed data using Bayes' theorem.
Posteriorx The posterior distribution represents the updated beliefs about the parameters of a model after incorporating observed data. It is derived by combining the prior distribution, which reflects initial beliefs about the parameter, with the likelihood of the observed data using Bayes' theorem.
Priorx A prior represents the initial belief or knowledge about an uncertain quantity, such as a model parameter, before observing any data. It is formally defined as a probability distribution that quantifies the degree of belief in the parameter's possible values based on previous information, expert opinion, or theoretical considerations.
Probability-Mass-Function A probability mass function (PMF) is a function that gives the probability that a discrete random variable is exactly equal to some value. The pmf is a mathematical function that gives the probability that a discrete random variable is exactly equal to some specific value. It is the primary way to define the probability distribution of a discrete random variable. (Brave-AI) Sometimes it is also known as probability function, frequency function or discrete probability density function. (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_mass_function">Wikipedia</a>)
Qwen-14b Qwen-14B is a 14-billion-parameter large language model developed by Alibaba Cloud as part of the Qwen (Tongyi Qianwen) series. It is a Transformer-based model pretrained on over 3 trillion tokens of diverse data, including web texts, books, code, mathematics, and multilingual content, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks.
Rate-Parameter The rate hyperparameter in the gamma distribution, typically denoted as β (beta), controls the scale of the distribution and is the inverse of the scale parameter (i.e., rate = 1/scale). A higher rate means events occur more frequently, leading to a narrower and more concentrated distribution; a lower rate implies less frequent events, resulting in a broader distribution. (Brave-AI)
rule-68–95–99 68–95–99.7 rule is a statistical shorthand used to remember the percentage of values that lie within specific intervals of a normal distribution. It states that approximately 68% of data falls within one standard deviation (σ) of the mean (μ), 95% within two standard deviations, and 99.7% within three standard deviations. This rule is also known as the empirical rule or the three-sigma rule.
Shape-Parameter The shape parameter in the context of the gamma distribution is a key hyperparameter that controls the form or shape of the distribution. It is often denoted as α (alpha). A higher shape parameter (α) results in a more peaked and right-skewed distribution; a lower shape parameter leads to a flatter, more spread-out distribution. (Brave-AI)
Weibull model The Weibull model is a statistical model where the response variable follows a Weibull distribution, which is appropriate for positive continuous data — particularly time-to-event data (survival times, failure times, lifetimes). (Brave-AI)
